title: BIMLOGIQ Argus: Revit AI Agent Capabilities and Evaluation
summary: Review BIMLOGIQ Argus documentation, its relationship to Copilot, supported Revit releases, and a practical evaluation of reusable commands.
body_markdown:
If you used BIMLOGIQ Copilot in Revit, Argus is the product it has become. BIMLOGIQ describes Argus as Copilot's successor. The main change is planning and chained tool use: Argus can break a request into steps and call several tools in sequence to complete it. A request like "create the sheets in this register on our title block" can then run as one job.


Below is what Argus does, how its approval step works, and where it fits next to other Revit AI tools.


## BIMLOGIQ Argus Revit AI agent


Argus works inside Revit as a conversational agent. BIMLOGIQ's documentation covers making model changes, working with supporting files, reviewing commands before they run, and saving commands so you can run them again ([Argus overview](https://bimlogiq.com/docs/copilot/docs/what-is-bimlogiq-copilot) ). The[BIMLOGIQ product page](https://bimlogiq.com/) lists support for Revit 2022 through 2027. That range matters if your office still keeps some projects on Revit 2022.


To install it, you sign in to a BIMLOGIQ account and activate a license, so check the current trial or commercial terms with BIMLOGIQ before you roll it out to a team ([Argus activation instructions](https://bimlogiq.com/docs/copilot/docs/how-to-install) ). If you search for help, be aware that older articles and videos may mention Copilot and describe an earlier version of the product. The Argus documentation is the current reference.


## Every command is shown before it runs


For a BIM manager, the approval step is the most useful thing about Argus. The documentation says that when you ask Argus for something, it generates a command and shows it to you for approval before anything runs.


This matters because an AI agent working in a live model can make a plausible change to the wrong elements. It might renumber every room on a level when you meant one wing, or write a value into an instance parameter when the type should have changed. With a review step you can catch that before it reaches the model. Finding it later in a schedule is much harder.


How much the preview helps depends on who reads it. Someone who knows the Revit API can read a command preview and see what the code will touch. A production architect or technician usually needs plain answers: which elements will change, which parameters, and what the new values will be. If your reviewers are in the second group, check whether the preview answers those questions before they approve. If it doesn't, narrow the request until the scope is obvious. Ambiguous instructions are where an agent is most likely to guess.


Reusable commands build on this. When a reviewed command has done what you wanted, you can save it and run it again instead of generating a new one each time. A saved command that has already been checked is a safer thing to hand to a colleague than a prompt they would have to reword and hope gives the same result.


## A worked example: sheets from an Excel register


Most projects keep their sheet list outside Revit, often in a spreadsheet the project architect updates before each issue. Turning that list into sheets is tedious. You create each sheet, pick the title block, type the number and name, and do it all again whenever the register changes.


BIMLOGIQ documents this as an Argus workflow ([Argus sheet creation and update guide](https://bimlogiq.com/docs/copilot/docs/create-sheets-from-excel) ). You point Argus at the Excel file, map the register's columns to sheet number and sheet name, and choose the title block for the new sheets. Argus then builds the sheets from the rows in the file, creating new ones and updating ones that already exist.


Look closely wherever the register and the model disagree. Revit requires every sheet number to be unique. A duplicate number in the spreadsheet, or a row whose number already belongs to a sheet with a different name, needs a person to decide what happens. After a run, compare the sheet list in the Project Browser with the register and make sure every row is accounted for.


The second run tells you more than the first. When the register is revised for the next issue, run it again, from a saved command if you kept one. Check that renamed sheets were updated in place and that no duplicates appeared. Creating a set of sheets once is a modest saving. A command that keeps up with every revision of the register for the rest of the project is worth much more.


## Where Argus fits


Argus is built for conversational Revit work, with an emphasis on reviewing and reusing commands. It also accepts PDFs, spreadsheets and cloud documents, according to[BIMLOGIQ's product overview](https://bimlogiq.com/) , so its work can start from the same outside material your team uses. Its Revit 2022 support counts in its favor if you maintain older projects.


For a team working across Revit and AutoCAD, ArchiLabs Desktop is another option. The main difference is application coverage. Desktop runs on Windows, edits native models in Revit 2023 through 2027, and works in AutoCAD. In the same conversation you can attach PDFs, spreadsheets, project documents, marked-up screenshots and narrated screen recordings. It starts at $19 a month plus usage credits ([pricing](https://archilabs.ai/pricing) ).


To compare the two directly, you could run the same sheet-register task in[Desktop](https://archilabs.ai/desktop) . Once that works, our[ten-task Revit comparison](https://archilabs.ai/posts/best-ai-revit-ten-task-comparison) covers a broader set of jobs to test.
